However, in early 2022, hyperscale operators scooped up much of the available real estate in primary data center markets [3], effectively shutting out smaller data center operators. Therefore, evaluation of secondary markets may be more fruitful for future siting considerations. One real estate caveat is that building in regions with a high potential for hurricanes, earthquakes, wildfires and other natural disasters puts your data and equipment at risk. These regions are often more expensive to build in due to added insurance and construction regulations, as well as improved structural hardening to offset risks, so there may be a point at which an area may not be worth the additional risk and expense [3, 7]. 3.5 Security Investment risk to the developer of the data center will require some attention to both cyber security and physical site security. This could be in the form of fences, barriers, 24/7 guarded site access, onsite security teams, and automated security. The site should be in a safe and secure area, away from high crime areas [1]. In addition, buildings and support equipment should be protected from fire and other natural disaster risks. Risk As noted, when considering the real estate cost, the risk of natural and man-made hazards to the site must be evaluated. A loss of the data center or a loss of access to the data center could negatively impact the 13 user base or force the operator to rely on a backup data center. By choosing a secure location, businesses can mitigate the risk of data loss and ensure the continuity of their operations [18]. Risks could include: • Commercial airports • Chemical or energy facilities (fire, missile, or toxic gas) • Seismic zones • Faults • Volcanic activity • High water (including climatic impacts) • High wind (including climatic impacts) • Fire threat (including climatic impacts) These and other identified risks should be flagged if they are within a certain distance of the proposed site or if they engulf a proposed site so that the siting decision is better informed. Data center siting should also consider any planned inter-connectivity with other data centers. An organization that offers a nationwide network of data centers can promise more reliability than one that has sites all within a short distance of one another. The ability of a datacenter to failover to another location after a disaster is an important siting consideration. From the user perspective, if an organization is choosing to house data in more than one data center, choosing facilities that are far enough apart means selecting centers that are not prone to the same risks. While there’s no hard or fast requirement, 100 miles is a good rule of thumb for data center separation for one organization [19]. All these parameters serve as flags in the siting decision process.
